source: Patel, Wang & Fan (2026) Deficient executive control in transformer attention (PNAS Nexus), methods
finding: The Stroop stimuli were PNG images of vertical word lists, not text. Four colours (RED, YELLOW, GREEN, BLUE), neutral words, nonword control. Models named the ink colour.
numbers: 30 unique random lists per list-length condition per model; lengths 1, 5, 10, 20, 40 words; congruent, incongruent, mixed (50/50), neutral, nonword.
quote: Stimuli text used the Arial font ... converted to images using a custom Visual Basic macro
limits: The collapse is a vision-language result. It was not shown for plain-text lists, and chunking the list in code was not tested, so gap 2 stays open.
agent_relevance: Do not read the 40-word collapse as a text-context rule. Test a text version before using it to set list or batch sizes (G11).

source: Patel, Wang & Fan (2026) PNAS Nexus, mixed-trial and incongruent results
finding: In mixed lists GPT-4o drifts toward reading the word instead of naming the colour as lists get longer. Word reading stays near perfect.
numbers: Incongruent: GPT-4o 91/57/22/15% at 5/10/20/40 words; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 76% at 20 and 24% at 40 (52-point drop). Mixed GPT-4o 100/99/72/52/41% at 1/5/10/20/40 words (about 50% is what a word-reading default gives). Congruent 99% at 20 words, 89% (GPT-4o) and 92% (Claude) at 40.
limits: n=30 lists per cell. No check of counting or format limits as a cause. One congruent anomaly (Claude 90 to 99% from 10 to 20 words) is explained by zero-correct trials.
agent_relevance: A competing habit beats the instruction more often as repeated material grows in one call. Keep the conflict-heavy part of a call short.

source: Patel, Wang & Fan (2026) PNAS Nexus, newer models
finding: GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro were tested 1-5 Sept 2025 with n=5. GPT-5 and Opus 4.1 improved slightly but still showed the deficit. Gemini 2.5 Pro was flat across conditions.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Pro: incongruent 72%, mixed 71%, neutral 73%, but nonword control only 40%. n=5 per model versus n=30 for the primary models.
limits: n=5 is too small for effect sizes. Per-model GPT-5 and Opus numbers sit in a supplementary table that I did not see.
agent_relevance: Frontier models are only weakly tested. Treat a run on our own model as required, not optional.

source: Patel, Wang & Fan (2026) PNAS Nexus, discussion of causes
finding: The authors offer only speculation for model differences: tokenization and no conflict-monitoring circuit. They do not test why Claude 3.5 Sonnet held to 20 words and GPT-4o did not. The congruency-sequence (Gratton) effect did not match the human pattern.
numbers: No experiment separates model size, training or format.
quote: Several factors may explain why results on the congruence sequence effect diverge from human behavioral patterns
limits: Gap 9 stays open. The model difference is descriptive only.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one vendor or model holds up longer; measure per model.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs (arXiv 2506.08184), model size
finding: About 35 models (0.6B to 405B, open and closed) show a log-linear decline in retrieving the latest value as updates per key grow from 3 to 400 (46 keys). The Interference Endurance Score (IES) is the area under accuracy versus log update count.
numbers: Parameter size class predicts IES significantly; nominal context window length does not. Reasoning models were left out of the regression because latency passed 200 s per task.
quote: an LLM's resilience to interference depends primarily on its overall representational capacity, not on how many tokens it can process
limits: Synthetic key-value task. Regression used open models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the slope is model-specific and size-driven. Measure it on our own model with the same recipe, then set steps before a forced reset from where accuracy crosses a chosen floor.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) arXiv 2506.08184, mitigation experiments
finding: Telling the model to forget, to focus forward, or to self-assess relevance gave marginal gains. Per-key forget moved errors to where the instruction sat, and hurt gpt-4.1-mini. A fake finished Q&A turn inserted 120 updates before the query ('mock QA reset') gave a substantial gain, though accuracy still fell with update count. A plain 'new session begins' cue was largely ineffective.
numbers: Five interventions, 46 keys, value length 6. Only the mock QA reset gave a large improvement.
quote: current LLMs cannot be reliably controlled through explicit natural-language user instructions alone
limits: The reset drops all earlier information, so it does not suit tasks that need selective access to history. Authors call it ad hoc.
agent_relevance: Supports S6: a hard boundary works, a spoken 'ignore the above' does not. Partly informs gap 1 but is not an equal-token fresh-vs-history test.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) arXiv 2506.08184, fixed-length and CoT experiments
finding: With input length held constant, tracking more keys cuts accuracy, longer values cut it faster, and chain-of-thought models did not beat their non-CoT versions.
numbers: llama4-maverick: near 100% tracking 2 keys, below 5% tracking 46. Value length 1 to 10 words: under 40% for every model; 40 words: under 5%. Stating where the answer is (activate-locate prompt) did not improve retrieval.
limits: Synthetic retrieval; real agent tasks may differ.
agent_relevance: Fewer items tracked per step helps directly. Keep live state small and move the rest to files or code.

source: Shnaidman (2026) Reset Is Not Recovery: Recoverability from False Conversational Context via Sycophancy Hysteresis (GroundLM workshop)
finding: After a user pushes a wrong answer, repairs that keep the history (user retraction, system reset, self-verification) recover only 2-3 of 14 model-dataset pairs. Removing the pressure history (fresh-context deletion or truncation) recovers 14 of 14.
numbers: 7 instruction-tuned open-weight models, 2 factual benchmarks. Oracle evidence with history kept: accuracy 0.368 to 0.929, wrong-answer following 41.2% to 4.3%. Controls rule out dialogue length, repeated confidence and plausible distractors.
quote: removing the pressure-bearing history entirely through fresh-context deletion or context truncation recovers all 14 of 14 pairs
limits: Abstract only. Open-weight models, multiple-choice factual QA, sycophancy not worry. Not an equal-token agent test but the closest direct comparison of rebuild versus carry-on found.
agent_relevance: Strong support for S6: delete the bad history rather than add a repair note. Gap 1 is partly closed for this failure type, open for our own agent and token budget.

source: Namboothiri (2026) Ghost Context: Measuring Cross-Context Interference in Long-Context Language Models (TrustNLP)
finding: Irrelevant spans make models cite real evidence from the wrong part of the input. Masking the single top-attributed distractor span fixes most detected errors.
numbers: 272 cases, 3 models. Strict Ghost Context Rate 38.3% for temporal contradictions; open-ended distractor influence in 20.4% of evaluations. Masking the top distractor resolves 95.5% of detected errors (Fix@1), 2.4% collateral damage, zero false positives on negative controls.
limits: Abstract only; model names not in it; small corpus; single author.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a code-side mask of the top distractor recovers about 95% of detected errors here. Supports filtering in code (G5) over telling the model to ignore.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2024) GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2410.05229)
finding: Adding one seemingly relevant clause that does not change the answer lowers accuracy by up to 65% across the state-of-the-art models tested. Changing only the numbers also lowers accuracy, and results vary across versions of the same problem.
numbers: Up to 65% drop (abstract). Per-model numbers were not in the abstract I read.
limits: Abstract only. 2024 models. A relevant-looking clause is a different manipulation from Shi 2023 distractor sentences.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: near-miss clauses still hurt later models than Shi 2023 used. Keep plausible but irrelevant text out of the call.

source: Gupta, Sheth, Raina, Gales & Fritz (2024) LLM Task Interference: An Initial Study on the Impact of Task-Switch in Conversational History (EMNLP)
finding: A direct task-switch test: a chat history from one task (up to 6 turns, correct answers forced) followed by a different target task. Many of the 15 switches lowered accuracy versus zero-shot; a few gave small gains. The authors define a task-switch sensitivity metric.
numbers: 5 datasets (Gigaword, MMLU abstract algebra, TweetQA, Rotten Tomatoes, MMLU HA), 15 switches, 4 models (Llama2-7b-chat, Mistral-7b-chat, GPT-3.5, GPT-4). Zero-shot MMLU AA accuracy: GPT-3.5 31.31, GPT-4 58.59, Llama 28.28, Mistral 21.21.
limits: The per-switch percent-change tables were garbled in the PDF text, so I do not quote them. Old models. Sensitivity could not be computed for closed models. One switch only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 (partly): a measured cost on a new task from old-task history. Supports a fresh context at each state change (S6). Still no flanker or WCST switch cost on modern models.

source: Challenging large language models' intelligence with human tools: a neuropsychological investigation in Italian (Heliyon 2024)
finding: Prefrontal-type tests (including Tower of London and Compound Remote Associates) were given to GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 2 and Llama 2 in Italian. GPT-3.5 and Claude 2 gave uneven profiles, Llama 2 was poor on almost all, GPT-4 was in the normative range except planning.
numbers: Four models; Tower of London used a one-shot chain-of-thought prompt. I found no Stroop, WCST or switching test among the tasks in the full text.
limits: Not a shifting or inhibition study; no switch cost. Older models.
agent_relevance: Shows human batteries can profile LLMs, but gap 3 is not closed by it.

source: Generalizable experiment agents threaten online behavioral experiments (OSF preprint 2026, AGEA)
finding: A general prompt-built agent completed 26 online experiments. On N-back, Tower of London and the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test it performed within typical human ranges, with accuracy and response time changing by condition.
numbers: 26 experiments, 7 platforms, 3 benchmark tasks. No perseveration or switch-cost figures in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. The agent drives a browser, so results mix vision, tool use and the model. No numbers to quote.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a modern agent can do WCST at human level, but no measured switch cost yet. Read the full preprint before relying on it.

source: Hao, Alexandre & Yu (2025) Visual Large Language Models Exhibit Human-Level Cognitive Flexibility in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (IEEE TCDS)
finding: Title and authors seen via Crossref only. The title claims visual LLMs reach human-level cognitive flexibility on WCST.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Could not open the paper. Do not cite beyond the title.
agent_relevance: Best lead for gap 3. Needs a full read for perseverative errors and prompting conditions.

source: Goto, Idei, Shiozuka & Ogata (2025) Performance of Large Language Models and Analysis of Responses in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (ICDL)
finding: Title and authors seen via Crossref only. Second WCST-on-LLM lead.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Lead for gap 3; needs reading.

source: Shi, Sharpe & Abbott (2019) A meta-analysis of the relationship between anxiety and attentional control (Clin Psychol Rev)
finding: Preregistered (PROSPERO CRD42016036927) test of ACT hypotheses. Deficits in efficiency not effectiveness; inhibition and switching but not updating; larger under high cognitive load.
numbers: 58 studies, N=8292, Hedges g=-0.58. Age moderated in behavioural studies; anxiety severity moderated in self-report studies.
limits: Abstract only. Moderator tables and the number of updating studies are not available, so gap 7 cannot be settled. A meta-analysis is not a preregistered replication of ACT.
agent_relevance: Keep the updating-under-anxiety claim contested.

source: Moran (2016) Anxiety and working memory capacity: A meta-analysis and narrative review (Psychol Bull)
finding: Anxiety relates to poorer working memory capacity across span types, largest on dynamic span.
numbers: 177 samples, N=22,061, g=-.334. Complex span -.342 (k=30, N=3,196); simple span -.318 (k=127, N=17,547); dynamic span (N-back) -.437 (k=20, N=1,318).
limits: Self-reported anxiety, capacity tasks. Shi codes 'updating' differently, so the two are not like for like. A coding difference is likely but unproven.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 leans to a coding difference (capacity in Moran, efficiency in Shi) but stays open. Do not import either as an agent rule.

source: Gillan et al. (2021) Experimentally induced and real-world anxiety have no demonstrable effect on goal-directed behaviour (Psychol Med)
finding: A strong anxiety induction (7.5% CO2) left goal-directed control unchanged. Real-life panic attacks and stressful events were also unrelated to it.
numbers: Exp 1 between-subject N=88; Exp 2 within-subject N=50; Exp 3 correlational N=1413.
quote: found no evidence that anxiety impairs goal-directed control in human subjects
limits: Goal-directed control is not shifting or inhibition. It is a boundary case for ACT-style claims, not a refutation.
agent_relevance: Caution: anxiety effects on control are task-specific. This weakens importing a general 'pressure hurts control' rule.

source: Eysenck, Moser, Derakshan, Hepsomali & Allen (2023) A neurocognitive account of attentional control theory (Cogn Emot)
finding: The theory authors' own update: efficiency is impaired through inefficient executive processes, framed with fronto-parietal, cingulo-opercular and default-mode networks. The abstract reports no new large replication.
numbers: No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only, written by the theory's authors. Gap 8 stays open: no large preregistered replication found.
agent_relevance: Treat ACT as a hypothesis source, not an engineering rule.

source: Cocks, Jackson, Bishop & Williams (2016) Anxiety, anticipation and contextual information: A test of attentional control theory (Cogn Emot)
finding: Tennis anticipation under high versus low anxiety: processing efficiency fell, response accuracy did not. The authors call it partial support for ACT.
numbers: Skilled and less-skilled players; efficiency = accuracy divided by mental effort. N not in the abstract.
limits: Small applied sample, sport task.
agent_relevance: Matches the efficiency-before-accuracy pattern. Check token use as well as accuracy under worry wording (gap 6).

source: Learning where to be flexible (OSF preprint 2022) and Cognitive flexibility versus stability via activation-based and weight-based adaptations (Communications Psychology 2026)
finding: People switch more efficiently in a high-switch environment, but environment-specific triggering of flexibility appeared only after four days of training, not one day. A recurrent network showed fast transient adaptation in activation space and slow lasting adaptation in weight space.
numbers: Human preprint: Exp 1 (1 day) N=52 no environment-specific effect; Exp 2 (4 days) N=51 effect. The 2026 paper was seen as a model abstract only.
limits: Abstracts via Crossref only; authorship not checked. The 2022 preprint may differ from the published version.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a scaffold with no weight change gets only the fast transient in-context adaptation, and it resets with each fresh context. Frequent S6 resets will not build a lasting benefit.
